questions.prompt: A booking team ships a shorter checkout form to reduce abandonment. Which measure best shows whether the product outcome improved?
choices: The number of fields removed from the form
The percentage of users who start checkout and complete a booking
The number of bookings opened by the support team
The percentage of rollout tasks finished on time
questions.explanation: Checkout completion measures the change in customer behavior the team wanted. Fields removed and tasks finished describe the work delivered, so either could improve even if customers still abandon checkout.

questions.prompt: A meal-delivery discount increases orders, but late deliveries and cancellations soon rise. What should the PM investigate first?
choices: Whether the larger order count still beats the acquisition target
Whether the discount can be displayed on more menu pages
Whether customers rate the discount message highly
Whether peak order volume exceeded kitchen or courier capacity
questions.explanation: Kitchen or courier capacity can become a bottleneck when a discount increases demand. Check volumes and wait times by stage. The acquisition target can show demand grew, but it cannot explain where orders became delayed.

questions.prompt: A team wants to make bookkeeping easier for freelancers. Which statement is a product strategy for that vision?
choices: Start with solo freelancers and differentiate through automatic expense categorization
Become the simplest bookkeeping product for every small business
Increase weekly bookkeeping completion from 35% to 50%
Build receipt scanning this quarter and bank import next quarter
questions.explanation: A strategy chooses whom to serve and how to deliver a distinctive benefit. The broad aspiration is a vision, the percentage target is an objective, and the sequence of builds is a roadmap.

questions.prompt: A grocery PM wants more customers to place a second order. Which measure is a plausible leading indicator to track alongside the 30-day repeat rate?
choices: The 30-day repeat rate measured at the end of next month
The annual contribution margin from repeat customers
The share of first orders delivered within the original promised window
The number of engineering tasks completed for delivery improvements
questions.explanation: First-order reliability is available soon after delivery and may influence whether someone returns. Validate that relationship before relying on it. Monthly repeat rate and annual margin take longer to observe, while task counts measure delivery work.

questions.prompt: A PM is comparing two initiatives with similar reach, impact, and effort. One estimate comes from a pilot and the other from a team guess. Which RICE input should reflect that difference?
choices: Reach
Confidence
Impact
Effort
questions.explanation: Confidence captures how much evidence supports the estimates. A pilot can justify higher confidence if it represents the target users. Impact measures the expected effect, even when the evidence for that estimate is weak.

questions.prompt: A commuter checks three transport apps after a train delay. Which statement best captures the job they are trying to get done?
choices: When a delay threatens my appointment, help me choose a route that gets me there on time
When I use a transit app, give me a tab with real-time delay notifications
When I miss a train, let me switch from a map to a timetable view
When I commute, give me a reason to use the same transit app daily
questions.explanation: The job combines a trigger, the user's motivation, and the progress they want. Delay notifications and timetable views are possible solutions. Either may work, depending on what information helps the commuter choose.

questions.prompt: A clinic manager buys scheduling software, while nurses use it during shifts. Which decision best reflects this distinction?
choices: Group the manager and nurses together because they use the same organization account
Use the number of employee accounts as the main way to segment users
Design the entire workflow around the manager because the manager chooses the vendor
Learn what the manager needs to buy and what nurses need to schedule visits under time pressure
questions.explanation: Buyers and daily users may have different goals and constraints. The manager may need approval and reporting features, while nurses may need quick scheduling. A shared account does not make those needs interchangeable.

questions.prompt: In five usability sessions, four shoppers open several product pages to compare delivery dates. Which statement is the best research insight to test next?
choices: Four of five shoppers opened more than one product page
Shoppers may need to compare delivery dates before choosing a product
Most shoppers in the entire market prefer delivery to in-store shopping
The catalog should add a calendar view to every product page
questions.explanation: An insight proposes an underlying need based on the observed pattern. The session count is an observation, and the calendar is a possible solution. Five sessions cannot establish how common a preference is across the market.

questions.prompt: You want to understand why some customers abandon identity verification. Which interview question is the best starting point?
choices: Would a more modern verification screen make you finish?
How frustrating did you find our document instructions?
Walk me through the last time you tried to verify your identity
Which of these three improvements would make you verify today?
questions.explanation: Asking for a recent experience invites a concrete sequence and lets unexpected barriers emerge. Rating the instructions or comparing proposed improvements too early can steer the answer toward a problem the team already suspects.

questions.prompt: A travel team believes showing the total fare earlier will reduce checkout abandonment. Which test best measures whether it changes real behavior?
choices: Compare checkout completion for randomly assigned customers who see early total fares or the current flow
Ask visitors whether early fares would make them more likely to book
Show a prototype and count how many people find the total fare
Release the change to everyone and compare the next holiday week with a normal week
questions.explanation: Random assignment gives the team a fair comparison of actual booking behavior. A prototype can show that people notice the price, while a holiday comparison may mix the effect of the change with seasonality.

questions.prompt: A workshop starts with a senior leader proposing a new dashboard. What should the facilitator do to get a wider range of ideas?
choices: Ask the team to improve the dashboard before generating other options
Have the group vote on the dashboard and brainstorm only if it loses
Restate the user need, have people sketch independently, then compare the options
Ask engineering to estimate the dashboard before inviting alternatives
questions.explanation: Independent ideation gives different ideas room to emerge before the team evaluates them. Estimating or voting on the first idea early tends to anchor the group around that option.

questions.prompt: A team is designing a medical appointment flow. What is the most useful addition to a user-flow map that already shows a successful booking?
choices: A final illustration for the confirmation screen
A list of database fields used by the scheduling service
A set of marketing headlines about the booking feature
A branch for no available slots that lets patients change the date or location
questions.explanation: A user flow should show decisions, failure states, and recovery options. No available slots is a realistic branch. Artwork or database details may matter later, but they cannot reveal whether the patient has a path forward.

questions.prompt: The team needs to learn whether customers understand when billing resumes after pausing a subscription. What is the smallest useful prototype?
choices: A clickable pause and confirmation flow with realistic billing dates
A working billing integration that pauses actual payments
A complete account settings redesign with all actions clickable
A survey with a list of possible subscription features
questions.explanation: A clickable flow lets people act and explain when they expect billing to resume. Real payments add effort and risk for a question about comprehension. A feature survey would measure preferences rather than understanding.

questions.prompt: A form turns invalid fields red and displays no other message. Which revision best helps users recognize and recover from an error?
choices: Use a stronger shade of red and add a red border around the form
Show plain-language guidance next to the field and keep a clear keyboard focus indicator
Show a generic error banner at the top and clear all field values
Replace the red border with a warning icon and leave the instructions unchanged
questions.explanation: Field-specific text explains what happened and how to fix it, while clear focus supports keyboard navigation. A different color or icon may draw attention but still leaves the correction unclear.

questions.prompt: A team plans to reduce first-order cancellations this quarter. Which item belongs in the product requirements document for its next release?
choices: The quarter-by-quarter sequence of every product bet
The running backlog of individual engineering tasks and bug fixes
The target shopper, success measure, delivery-window requirements, and what is out of scope
The company’s long-term ambition to become the most dependable marketplace
questions.explanation: A product requirements document defines the problem, target users, desired outcome, and what the release must do. A roadmap sequences strategic bets, and a backlog breaks them into smaller tasks.

questions.prompt: A repair marketplace wants a North Star metric tied to recurring customer value. Which metric fits best?
choices: Weekly ad impressions for repair listings
Weekly repair requests created
Weekly customer-support conversations
Weekly repair jobs completed with no unresolved issue
questions.explanation: A completed repair with no unresolved issue represents value the customer received. A request is a useful input, but requests can rise while too few repairs are completed.

questions.prompt: A grocery app reports on-time delivery among delivered orders. The rate rises while cancellations double. What should the team report alongside the improved rate?
choices: Cancellations per placed order, using the same time window
The number of new products added during the month
The highest on-time rate achieved by any store
Average delivery time for orders that arrived early
questions.explanation: The reliability denominator excludes cancelled orders. Reporting the cancellation rate alongside it reveals whether more failed orders disappeared from the denominator. A best-store result can hide the same problem.

questions.prompt: Shoppers often start an order on a phone and finish on a laptop. How should an A/B test of the checkout flow assign returning shoppers?
choices: Randomly assign the checkout version on each page visit
Assign the new version to phone sessions and the current version to laptop sessions
Randomly assign each eligible customer account once and keep its version consistent
Switch the checkout version for everyone at the start of each day
questions.explanation: A stable account-level assignment keeps the same shopper in one group across devices. Randomizing every visit can expose a shopper to both versions and make it harder to attribute the outcome.

questions.prompt: The March signup cohort has had 30 days to return, but the April cohort has only had 12. How can you compare repeat usage now?
choices: Compare March’s 30-day rate with April’s 12-day rate
Compare both cohorts at the same age since signup, such as day 12
Assume the rest of April will repeat at the same rate as March
Use the number of returning users without comparing cohort sizes
questions.explanation: Align cohorts by time since the starting event. Comparing both at day 12 gives each user the same observation window. April’s 30-day rate can be calculated once that cohort has had time to mature.

questions.prompt: A tutoring marketplace is assessing whether teacher referrals form a growth loop. What would demonstrate a loop?
choices: A paid campaign drives many teachers to sign up one time
Students see more ads after each lesson ends
Returning teachers spend longer editing their profiles
Completed lessons attract new teachers, who improve availability and help generate more completed lessons
questions.explanation: A growth loop exists when the output of one cycle helps produce the next cycle. Here, completed lessons attract supply and better supply generates more lessons. A one-time campaign can acquire users without creating that feedback.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery case reports more dinner cancellations. Which analysis best helps decide what to fix first?
choices: Compare this month's total dinner orders with last month's total
Break cancellations down by stage, who cancelled, and peak versus off-peak orders
Compare average delivery time for only the orders that were completed
Measure how many customers opened the restaurant list
questions.explanation: Breaking cancellations down by timing, actor, and operating conditions distinguishes different failure modes. Completed-order delivery times can be useful, but they exclude the orders that failed.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking case finds many users leave after seeing a late-added service fee. Which primary metric should a total-price test track?
choices: The percentage of eligible searchers who confirm a booking
The number of taps on the fare breakdown
The average time users spend comparing itineraries
The number of prices displayed on search results
questions.explanation: Confirmed bookings per eligible searcher measure the goal of completing more bookings. Fare-breakdown taps indicate interaction, but can rise without conversion improving. Monitor cancellations and margin as guardrails.

questions.prompt: A game’s redesigned tutorial increases average first-session length. Which result would better support a claim of meaningful engagement?
choices: Players spend more time on the tutorial settings screen
More players open the shop before starting a match
More new players complete a first match and return on day 7
More tutorial messages appear per session
questions.explanation: Completing a match reflects experiencing the game, and returning provides evidence that the value lasted beyond the tutorial. Longer sessions can also result from confusion, so duration alone is ambiguous.

questions.prompt: You’re writing a portfolio case about a checkout prototype that never launched. How should you describe the impact?
choices: Quote a benchmark conversion lift as the prototype’s expected result without labeling it
Report the team's projected revenue as measured business impact
Omit the prototype because a case study needs production numbers
Label projections and simulated data, describe your work, and explain how you would validate impact
questions.explanation: A simulated case can show strong product reasoning if it distinguishes assumptions, actual work, and evidence still needed. Presenting projected results as measured outcomes would misrepresent the case.

questions.prompt: A mentor says your case jumps from a customer quote to a feature proposal. What is the most useful revision?
choices: Show the recurring evidence, explain its limits, compare alternatives, and justify the chosen test
Add more screenshots of the proposed feature to make it easier to picture
Replace the quote with a longer quote from the same interview
Add a projected revenue figure before the recommendation
questions.explanation: The feedback points to a missing reasoning step. Connect the observed pattern to a need, show where the evidence is uncertain, and explain why the selected idea deserves a test. More polished artifacts cannot supply that missing reasoning.

questions.prompt: A grocery item appears available in a cached search result. A shopper adds it to their cart five minutes later. What should the team require at checkout?
choices: Carry the search result into checkout and show when it was last refreshed.
Let the mobile app calculate remaining stock from the shopper’s cart.
Have the checkout service recheck authoritative inventory and handle a stock change.
Increase the search cache refresh rate and use the displayed result for payment.
questions.explanation: A cached result helps the shopper browse quickly. Checkout needs the authoritative inventory record because other shoppers can buy the item between searches. Specify what the shopper sees if the item becomes unavailable.

questions.prompt: A payment request times out after the shopper taps Pay. Which recovery behavior best reduces the risk of a duplicate charge?
choices: Check the original payment status and reuse the same idempotency key for a permitted retry.
Retry immediately with a new payment identifier and reconcile duplicate charges later.
Treat the timeout as a decline and create a new payment when the shopper tries again.
Show payment success and let fulfillment confirm whether a charge arrived.
questions.explanation: A timeout leaves the original outcome unknown. A status check can reveal that the payment already succeeded, and reusing the key allows a supported retry to refer to the same operation. A new identifier can create a second payment.

questions.prompt: A branch contains an approved checkout copy change and an unrelated experimental configuration edit. What should the author do before requesting review?
choices: Stage both edits and explain in the review description which one is experimental.
Commit both edits, then ask the reviewer to check only the checkout screenshots.
Merge the copy change and use the review to document the remaining configuration edit.
Inspect the diff, stage only the copy change, and open a pull request with test evidence.
questions.explanation: Git commits the staged changes. Inspecting and staging only the intended edit keeps the pull request focused and makes the test evidence easier to interpret. A description cannot remove an unrelated edit from the diff.

questions.prompt: A concert ticket service is preparing for a surge at the opening of a sale. Which design best helps it serve shoppers while keeping purchases accurate?
choices: Send every purchase directly to the database and raise the retry rate when it slows.
Cache event details, queue purchase requests, and check authoritative inventory at purchase.
Cache the number of unsold seats and confirm purchases from that count during the surge.
Queue event-detail reads while keeping the purchase service open to unlimited retries.
questions.explanation: Caching reduces repeated reads for event details, and a queue lets the service process purchases at a manageable rate. The authoritative inventory check protects against selling the same seat twice. A cached seat count can lag behind real purchases.

questions.prompt: A small clinic is launching appointment reminders. One team owns the application and database. When would separating reminders into their own service make the strongest sense?
choices: The reminder feature has a different color palette from appointment booking.
The team wants each new feature to have a separate repository from day one.
Reminder traffic repeatedly needs to scale separately and its failures affect booking.
The team wants a faster first release and expects little reminder traffic initially.
questions.explanation: Independent scaling and failure isolation can justify a separate service. A single application is often simpler to ship and debug at the start, so a split should address an observed operational or ownership need.

questions.prompt: Only 4% of orders arrive late. A model labels every order on time and reaches 96% accuracy. If the team wants to intervene on likely late orders, what should it check first?
choices: The percentage of on-time orders the model correctly labels on time.
Recall for late orders and the precision of flags at a workable alert threshold.
Accuracy on a second sample with the same share of late orders.
Average delivery duration for orders without an alert.
questions.explanation: Recall shows how many actual late orders the model catches. Precision shows how many alerts point to actual late orders and helps the team judge workload. Overall accuracy can look high because on-time orders dominate the data.

questions.prompt: A team wants an LLM to summarize 800 survey comments and report how many mention fees. How should it produce a dependable count?
choices: Ask the model to estimate the share from a handful of representative comments.
Ask the model twice and average the counts from the two summaries.
Use a longer prompt and accept the count if the explanation reads clearly.
Define the theme, verify comment labels, and calculate the total from those labels in code or a spreadsheet.
questions.explanation: A verified set of labels gives the team a count it can reproduce, and the model can explain that result. Averaging two generated numbers does little to resolve a shared miscount or a vague definition of what qualifies.

questions.prompt: A support model must classify tickets as refund, delivery, or account. Some messages contain too little information. Which design makes the output easiest to evaluate and use?
choices: Define the labels, request a supporting phrase and an unknown option, and validate the output format.
Require one label for every message and accept the model’s confidence as the deciding factor.
Let the model create new categories whenever a message seems ambiguous.
Provide examples of well-written replies and parse the category from a generated paragraph.
questions.explanation: Explicit labels and a validated format create a repeatable contract. A supporting phrase and an unknown option make ambiguous tickets easier to review. Forcing a category can turn missing evidence into a guess.

questions.prompt: Refund rules differ by region and change monthly. Which approach best supports a customer-facing answer about the rule that applies today?
choices: Fine-tune on last quarter’s support replies and let the model infer updates from the customer’s question.
Retrieve the most popular refund article without filtering by order type or region.
Retrieve the active policy for the order’s region and type, cite it, and escalate if evidence is missing.
Include archived policy versions and let the model choose the passage with the closest wording.
questions.explanation: Retrieval at answer time can supply the policy that is active for the specific order. Fine-tuning can improve a stable behavior such as formatting, but it cannot guarantee that a changing policy is current.

questions.prompt: A policy assistant retrieves the correct scanned PDF page, but repeatedly cites the eligibility limit from an adjacent plan in a table. Where should the team investigate first?
choices: The answer template’s citation style and the placement of the reference link.
Whether OCR and chunking preserve the table headers, rows, and plan-to-limit relationships.
How many additional policy pages the model can fit into its context window.
Whether to fine-tune on more examples of confident eligibility answers.
questions.explanation: The correct page can still become misleading if extraction separates values from their row and column labels. Compare the retrieved text with the original table and preserve its structure. Retrieving more pages will leave the broken relationship in place.

questions.prompt: A dispatch agent finds three routes that all meet delivery windows. It ranks them by fuel use, courier workload, and lateness risk. Which pattern is it using to choose a route?
choices: A simple reflex rule triggered by the most recent courier update.
A model-based rule that maintains an internal picture of courier locations.
A goal-based planner that accepts any route meeting the delivery windows.
A utility-based planner that compares trade-offs among acceptable routes.
questions.explanation: Meeting the delivery windows is the goal. Ranking feasible routes by their costs and benefits adds a utility function, which helps choose among options that satisfy the same goal.

questions.prompt: A scheduling assistant remembers that a learner usually prefers mornings. What should it use to propose an appointment for next Tuesday?
choices: The learner’s preferred time from their last session as proof that the slot is open.
The remembered preference to rank options and the live calendar to verify availability.
The last calendar result held in working memory as the schedule for next Tuesday.
The booking policy alone to decide which time is both preferred and open.
questions.explanation: Persistent memory can retain a useful preference. Availability changes, so verify it in the calendar before making a proposal. A preference or an earlier result is insufficient evidence that a slot is open.

questions.prompt: A support agent can look up orders and issue refunds. Which design best controls the risk of refunding the wrong person or amount?
choices: Give the agent access to all refunds and rely on a prompt that lists the policy exceptions.
Hide the refund button in the chat interface while allowing unrestricted backend calls.
Verify order ownership and eligibility in application code, limit tool permissions, and require approval where needed.
Let the agent process refunds and rely on the finance team’s weekly review to catch errors.
questions.explanation: Application-level checks and scoped tool permissions prevent unauthorized actions at the point of execution. Review logs are useful after the fact, but an unrestricted tool can still move money before anyone reviews it.

questions.prompt: An agent keeps quoting expired delivery guidance even though the current policy exists. Its context includes years of archived documents. What change is most likely to help?
choices: Pass the current policy, relevant order fields, and the question, with source and version information.
Include every policy version and ask the model to choose the one that sounds most recent.
Send the full conversation history and give the model more room to generate its reply.
Send only the policy document titles to make the context shorter.
questions.explanation: Context engineering selects the evidence needed for this decision. Supplying the active rule and its version reduces ambiguity, while an archive can crowd out the applicable passage or supply conflicting rules.

questions.prompt: A team connects an MCP server that can search approved policies and edit customer records. The first workflow only answers policy questions. What should the team do?
choices: Expose both tools because a standardized protocol establishes the caller’s business permissions.
Expose both tools and let the model decide whether a question authorizes a record edit.
Disable policy search until the same workflow can safely edit every relevant record.
Verify the server and its data flows, then grant the workflow access to policy search only.
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes how applications discover and connect to capabilities. The host still decides which operations a workflow may use. A policy-answering workflow needs read access and has no reason to receive a record-editing permission.

questions.prompt: A business analyst documents that recruiters enter candidate details twice. Which next step best demonstrates product management in a portfolio case?
choices: Compare the problem with other bottlenecks, choose a change to test, and measure speed and submission quality.
Expand the process map and treat stakeholder approval of the map as the outcome.
Write implementation requirements for the first idea and count completed tickets.
Estimate the time saved by automation and use the estimate as the reported result.
questions.explanation: A product case shows how evidence led to prioritization, a test, and a decision. Mapping the process is useful input. Completed tickets and untested estimates leave the effect on recruiters and submission quality unresolved.

questions.prompt: A clinic is considering automated reminders to reduce missed appointments. Which cross-functional plan gives the team the strongest evidence before committing?
choices: Have engineering choose the delivery channel first and ask design to write the message later.
Ask operations to select reminder timing and use a satisfaction survey as the only baseline.
Have design explore patient needs, engineering check scheduling integration, data establish no-show rates, and operations assess support impact.
Ask data to predict the launch impact and bring design and operations in once the rollout date is set.
questions.explanation: Each partner resolves a different uncertainty. Involving them early connects usability, feasibility, the outcome baseline, and operational risk before the team commits to a channel or launch plan.

questions.prompt: An AI screening pilot reduces reviewer time, but the team worries it may miss qualified applicants. What should the product manager require before expanding it?
choices: A lower cost per application and enough throughput to replace the current review step.
A comparison with the existing review process, measurement of missed qualified applicants, and a way for reviewers to correct decisions.
A high overall agreement rate with prior decisions and a survey of reviewer satisfaction.
More training examples from the same applicant pool and a faster average response time.
questions.explanation: The baseline shows what changed, and measuring missed qualified applicants targets the consequential failure. Overall agreement can look high even when a small but important group of qualified people is missed.

questions.prompt: A case interviewer asks you to improve a grocery app and offers no further details. What is the strongest first move?
choices: Propose a loyalty feature and describe how engineering could build it.
List competitor features and choose the one that would be quickest to copy.
Sketch a redesigned checkout and use stakeholder feedback to pick the target segment later.
Clarify the goal and constraints, choose a user segment, then locate a problem along its journey.
questions.explanation: The right product decision depends on the goal and who is struggling. Mapping the chosen segment’s journey creates a basis for asking where the problem occurs and what evidence would distinguish its causes.

questions.prompt: A PRD says checkout should show a transparent fee estimate. Which addition makes that requirement easiest to build and verify?
choices: Specify when itemized fees appear, how an expired coupon changes the total, and what happens if the pricing service times out.
Add several polished mockups and let the team decide exception behavior during implementation.
State that shoppers should trust checkout and track satisfaction after the release.
List the pricing service dependencies and leave estimate timing for the launch review.
questions.explanation: A testable PRD spells out the trigger, expected behavior, and important exceptions. A broad outcome such as trust is useful for measurement, while concrete acceptance behavior tells the team what to build and test.

questions.prompt: Design takes 3 days. After design, implementation takes 4 days and training takes 3 days in parallel. Testing takes 2 days after implementation. Both training and testing must finish before launch. What is the earliest finish?
choices: After 7 working days.
After 8 working days.
After 9 working days.
After 12 working days.
questions.explanation: The longest required chain is design, implementation, and testing, which takes 3 + 4 + 2 = 9 days. Training finishes after 6 days because it runs in parallel. Adding training to the longest chain would count time twice.

questions.prompt: Midway through a one-city delivery-window pilot, a sponsor asks for live courier tracking. What is the most useful response from the project lead?
choices: Estimate the effects on scope, schedule, and the experiment, then record the sponsor’s decision among clear options.
Add tracking to the pilot immediately and revise the launch date once engineers finish estimating it.
Keep the launch date and ask engineers to fit tracking into the existing work without revisiting scope.
Defer tracking until the pilot ends and skip documenting it because the current scope is already approved.
questions.explanation: A change can affect both delivery and what the pilot measures. An impact estimate helps the decision owner compare adding, replacing, or deferring work. Recording the decision keeps the team aligned on scope.

questions.prompt: Last week the team recorded a possible store-feed outage. Today the feed stopped updating and customers are seeing stale delivery estimates. How should the team handle the situation?
choices: Keep it in the risk register and raise the probability for the next weekly review.
Remove the risk entry because the team already documented what could happen.
Wait for more affected customers before assigning an owner to investigate it.
Manage it as an active issue, assign an owner, apply the planned fallback, and communicate the impact.
questions.explanation: A risk is a possible event. The outage has occurred and is affecting customers, so the team needs an active issue response with an owner, mitigation, and timely communication. Updating a probability alone does not restore service.

questions.prompt: The checkout pilot looks correct on screen, but the analyst finds the key tracking event is missing. The goal is to learn whether an earlier estimate reduces cancellations. What should happen next?
choices: Launch as planned and estimate the missing event from support messages after the pilot.
Treat event verification as a launch dependency, repair it, and verify it in the staff pilot before inviting customers.
Launch to a larger group so the extra traffic compensates for the missing event.
Change the pilot’s primary metric to page views because that event is already recorded.
questions.explanation: The pilot needs reliable data to answer its original question. Verifying the event in a smaller staff pilot protects the customer rollout and makes the results interpretable. A larger sample cannot fix missing measurement.

questions.prompt: The team delivered the approved pilot and met the acceptance criteria. The cancellation result still needs two more weeks of data. How should the project lead close the work?
choices: Declare the customer outcome achieved because the deliverables met the acceptance criteria.
Keep every delivery task open until the outcome data are conclusive.
Close the agreed delivery scope, hand off support and monitoring, and assign an owner and date for the outcome review.
Archive the project after launch and leave future analysis to whoever next reviews cancellations.
questions.explanation: Project closure confirms delivery and transfers ownership. The product outcome is a separate question that still needs evidence, so the team should agree on who reviews it and when. Acceptance criteria alone do not establish impact.

questions.prompt: A product manager wants a weekly count of orders placed, including canceled orders. Which table should supply the starting rows?
choices: order_items, which has one row per order line
orders, which has one row per order
customers, which has one row per customer
events, which has one row per logged interaction
questions.explanation: The metric counts orders, so use a table with one row per order and keep canceled rows in the denominator. Order lines can repeat the same order, and a single customer can place several orders.

questions.prompt: Some acquisition channels were never recorded and are stored as NULL. Which filter selects those customers?
choices: WHERE acquisition_channel = NULL
WHERE acquisition_channel = ''
WHERE acquisition_channel IS NOT NULL
WHERE acquisition_channel IS NULL
questions.explanation: IS NULL matches missing values. An equality comparison with NULL evaluates to unknown, while an empty string is a known value and may represent a different data quality problem.

questions.prompt: A week has 16 orders created, of which 12 were completed by 10 distinct buyers. If completion rate is completed orders divided by orders created, what is the rate?
questions.explanation: Divide 12 completed orders by 16 created orders to get 75%. The 10 buyers describe a different grain, and filtering the denominator to completed orders would make the rate 100% by definition.

questions.prompt: You need a report showing the number of completed orders for every customer, including customers with zero. Which approach preserves the zeroes?
choices: INNER JOIN to completed orders and count order IDs
LEFT JOIN to all orders, filter to completed orders in WHERE, and count order IDs
LEFT JOIN with completed status in ON and count matching order IDs
LEFT JOIN with completed status in ON and count rows with COUNT(*)
questions.explanation: Putting the status condition in ON keeps customers who have no match. COUNT(order_id) ignores the NULL on their unmatched row and returns zero. COUNT(*) would count that placeholder row, and a WHERE filter on status would remove it.

questions.prompt: Two orders each total 1,500 cents. One order has two item rows and the other has one. How should you report total sales after bringing in item data?
choices: Use SUM(total_cents) on the three joined rows to report 4,500 cents
Aggregate item data to one row per order before joining, then report 3,000 cents
Use SUM(DISTINCT total_cents) on the joined rows to report 1,500 cents
Average the two order totals to report 1,500 cents
questions.explanation: Each order contributes its total once, so sales are 3,000 cents. A one-to-many join repeats order values, while SUM(DISTINCT total_cents) would also collapse separate orders that happen to have the same amount.

questions.prompt: Your order timestamps use fixed-width UTC text with second precision. Which date range captures every instant in February 2025 and excludes March 1?
questions.explanation: The half-open interval includes the first instant of February and excludes the March boundary. An upper bound at the start of February 28 misses later orders that day. An inclusive March boundary can overlap the next report.

questions.prompt: You have filtered the data to completed orders. You want to show the previous order date for each row, and orders can share a timestamp. Which window expression gives the right comparison?
choices: LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id)
LAG(created_at) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id)
LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC)
MAX(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)
questions.explanation: LAG looks at the previous row in the window. Partitioning keeps each customer's history separate, and the order ID breaks timestamp ties. Without the partition, the prior row could be another customer's purchase.

questions.prompt: An ordered funnel counts browse, then checkout, then purchase in the same session. Session A browses, checks out twice, and purchases. Session B browses, purchases, then checks out. Session C browses and purchases without checkout. How many sessions complete the funnel?
choices: Three sessions
Two sessions
Zero sessions
One session
questions.explanation: Only session A has all three events in the required order. Repeated checkouts count once at session grain. Session B's purchase is too early, and session C skips the checkout step.

questions.prompt: You report next-calendar-month retention by first purchase cohort. Data ends on March 15. What should you do with the February cohort when comparing mature retention rates?
choices: Include it and classify every buyer who has not returned by March 15 as unretained
Exclude it from the mature comparison until the full March follow-up is observable
Calculate its rate using only buyers who returned before March 15
Combine it with January so both cohorts share the same observation period
questions.explanation: February buyers need the full month of March to have the same follow-up opportunity as earlier cohorts. Reporting halfway through March or restricting the denominator to returners would bias the comparison.

questions.prompt: Your data extract starts April 1. A customer's earliest visible completed order is April 9, and they order again in May. What should you verify before calling them a retained April first-time buyer?
choices: Whether April 9 was their highest-value order
Whether they ordered the same items in May
Whether an earlier completed order exists outside the extract
Whether April and May contain the same number of calendar days
questions.explanation: The earliest visible order may be a repeat purchase if earlier history was cut off. Check historical coverage or an authoritative first-purchase field before assigning the customer to an acquisition cohort.

questions.prompt: A grocery service can reliably deliver evening slots in two neighborhoods. Families there report repeated dinner-planning problems. A larger group of commuters wants immediate lunch delivery across the city. Which initial segment is the stronger test?
choices: Citywide commuters, because the larger group gives the strongest launch signal
Both groups, using one delivery promise to keep the pilot simple
Every household in the city, using waitlist signups to confirm fit
Families in the two neighborhoods, where the team can test a recurring need with a promise it can fulfill
questions.explanation: The families are reachable, share a recurring need, and can be served with existing capacity. A larger audience is less informative when the team cannot reliably deliver what that audience values.

questions.prompt: Customers often abandon a grocery delivery app when they need ingredients by dinner. What should a positioning study compare?
choices: Only the features and prices of the leading grocery delivery apps
The actual alternatives customers choose, such as visiting a nearby store, and the trade-offs behind those choices
The acquisition channels and advertising budgets of similar apps
The proposed feature against the current app, using only a preference survey
questions.explanation: A trip to the store competes for the same customer job even though it is a different kind of service. Studying recent choices reveals the criteria the positioning needs to address, such as timing, certainty, and cost.

questions.prompt: A first-order discount doubles signups for a weekly grocery service. Which follow-up is stronger evidence of product–market fit?
choices: Measure how many people clicked the campaign ad
Ask new signups whether they would recommend the service
Compare repeat completed orders and willingness to pay within the target segment across equally mature cohorts
Count all first orders during the discount and compare them with the previous week's total
questions.explanation: For a weekly service, repeat use and willingness to pay indicate whether customers keep choosing it after acquisition. Equally mature cohorts have the same chance to return. A discount spike can show interest without durable value.

questions.prompt: You are deciding whether to redesign first-order checkout. Which research plan gives the strongest evidence about where shoppers struggle?
choices: Recruit customers who completed, abandoned, or used another option, then ask each to walk through their last attempt
Recruit loyal shoppers and ask whether a faster checkout sounds appealing
Recruit only people who abandoned and ask them to choose a preferred new design
Survey website visitors about which checkout features they expect to use
questions.explanation: Recruiting across outcomes lets you compare where the experience worked, broke down, or lost to an alternative. Asking about a recent attempt gives concrete behavior. Loyal shoppers alone may miss the barriers that drove others away.

questions.prompt: Of 8,000 eligible monthly checkout users, 25% experience a delivery estimate problem. A fix will reach half of those shoppers and is expected to raise completion by 4 percentage points among them. How many additional monthly orders does the estimate imply?
choices: 80 additional orders
200 additional orders
320 additional orders
40 additional orders
questions.explanation: The fix reaches 8,000 × 25% × 50%, or 1,000 shoppers. Apply the 4-point lift to those 1,000 shoppers to estimate 40 additional orders. Applying it to all affected users would assume full reach.

questions.prompt: Your objective is to make first orders more dependable. Which statement is the most useful key result for the pilot?
choices: Raise the share of eligible first deliveries arriving within the promised window from 78% to 87% by quarter end
Launch the updated checkout estimate by quarter end
Review the delivery dashboard with the team once a week
Add a support workflow for late first deliveries
questions.explanation: This key result defines an observable outcome with a baseline, a target, a population, and a deadline. Launching a feature or changing a workflow is an initiative. It may improve delivery reliability, but shipping it alone does not show that it did.

questions.prompt: A delivery-window experiment measures conversion per eligible shopper. The exposure event may fire more than once when checkout retries. What should the analytics contract specify?
choices: Use every exposure event as a denominator row and record only the timestamp
Count only shoppers with a purchase and record their checkout session ID
Record a stable assignment ID and firing rule, then use one eligible assignment row per shopper in the denominator
Fire the exposure event when checkout loads and count one row per event per day
questions.explanation: A stable assignment ID and clear firing rule let the team detect retries and match exposures to the experiment. One eligible assignment per shopper keeps the denominator at the intended grain. Counting every event would overweight shoppers who retry.

questions.prompt: During a limited checkout pilot, some shoppers see delivery times after the store closes. The rollout plan lists that failure as an immediate stop condition. What should the rollout owner do?
choices: Wait for the planned review and compare the overall conversion rates
Pause the rollout, confirm the faulty estimates are no longer shown, and investigate before restarting
Expand to more stores to see how widespread the failure is
Continue the pilot and add support instructions for shoppers affected by the error
questions.explanation: The stop condition covers a service promise the team cannot fulfill. Pausing limits further harm, and checking the rollback confirms the bad estimates are gone. A positive conversion trend would not resolve the broken promise.

questions.prompt: Two pricing groups each have 1,000 eligible shoppers. Price A produces 250 orders at $4 contribution each. Price B produces 200 orders at $6 each. What does the observed result show?
choices: Price A generated more contribution per eligible shopper because more orders were placed
The prices generated the same contribution per eligible shopper because the audience sizes matched
Price B generated $6 of contribution per eligible shopper and should be rolled out immediately
Price B lowered conversion and increased contribution per eligible shopper from $1.00 to $1.20
questions.explanation: Divide total contribution by all eligible shoppers. Price A yields 250 × $4 ÷ 1,000, or $1.00. Price B yields 200 × $6 ÷ 1,000, or $1.20. Contribution per order uses a different denominator, and rollout still depends on uncertainty and guardrails.

questions.prompt: Overall 30-day retention falls, yet retention increases within both major acquisition channels. More new customers came from the channel with the lower retention baseline. What should you bring to the decision review?
choices: A comparison at a fixed channel mix, along with cohort sizes and eligibility checks
A plan to roll back the product update based on the overall decline
Only the two channel trends, since the overall change no longer matters
A recommendation to expand the lower-retention channel because its rate rose
questions.explanation: The overall rate can fall when more customers come from a channel with a lower baseline, even as both channels improve. Comparing at a fixed mix helps separate composition from within-channel changes. The overall result still matters for the business.
